10/13/2026
UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA
ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
Vv. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Rossie D. Alston Jr.

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF’S RULE 72(a) OBJECTIONS TO ECF
NO. 84 AND MOTION TO SET ASIDE THE AMENDMENT AND DISCOVERY
DENIALS AND FOR COORDINATED DETERMINATION OF THE PENDING

OBJECTIONS

I. ECF NO. 84 TREATED THE RULE 26(d)(1) EXCEPTION AS UNAVAILABLE
AND DENIED A COMPLETED AMENDMENT SUBMISSION FOR
NONPRODUCTION OF A COMPARISON
ECF No. 84 denied ECF Nos. 15 and 54 on the stated ground that discovery had not begun

and would not begin until a Scheduling Order issued. ECF No. 84 at 1-2. ECF Nos. 15 and 54
asked for one thing: an order under Rule 26(d)(1) authorizing seven interrogatories before the Rule
26(f) conference. Rule 26(d)(1) permits discovery before that conference “when authorized . . . by
court order.” The motions invoked that clause. The Order treated the exception as absent. Part ITI

quotes the Order’s reasoning and answers it.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document91 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 2 of 29 PagelD# 906

The same Order denied ECF No. 59 for nonproduction of the comparison directed by ECF
No. 64. ECF No. 84 at 2. Plaintiff produced no comparison through October 7, 2026. He states that
without qualification. The objection concerns what that fact justified on this record. The complete
proposed pleading and a memorandum locating its material changes were on the docket; the
comparison condition was under timely challenge before this Court; relief from the expired
deadline was pending; and further amendment briefing had been accepted. ECF Nos. 59-1, 60, 66,
67, 68, 82. None of those requests was decided. ECF No. 84 disposed of them by denying the
motion they concerned.

Plaintiff asks the Court to set aside both rulings, to decide the comparison condition
together with the September objections, and to grant ECF Nos. 59, 15, and 54 on their existing
submissions or restore them for determination under the correct frameworks. Plaintiff separately
objects to ECF No. 84 on a ground that arose from financial disclosure reports he obtained after its
entry; Part IX states that objection. Plaintiff submits no comparison with this filing.

Il. EACH RULING IS REVIEWED UNDER THE STANDARD THAT GOVERNS IT,
AND THE OBJECTIONS ARE TIMELY
A. The standard separates legal premises, factual findings, and the exercise of
discretion.

The District Judge “must consider timely objections and modify or set aside any part of the
order that is clearly erroneous or is contrary to law.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 72(a); see 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)
(1)(A). The Fourth Circuit applies that text to nondispositive orders, and a court abuses its
discretion “when it relies on erroneous factual or legal premises.” Wall v. Rasnick, 42 F.4th 214,
217, 220 (4th Cir. 2022) (quoting United States v. Nicholson, 676 F.3d 376, 383 (4th Cir. 2012)).
Wall vacated a judgment entered after Rule 72(a) objections were overruled by implication without

resolution of the issues they raised. Id. at 216-18.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document91_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 3 of 29 PagelD# 907

Three kinds of error are presented. The first is legal: the premise that the absence of a
Scheduling Order and of ordinary discovery forecloses a Rule 26(d)(1) order. The second is
factual, to the extent the finding of “ample opportunity” rests on a misunderstanding of when
Plaintiff received notice of ECF No. 64. The third concerns discretion: whether denial of a
completed amendment submission was a permissible response to nonproduction on this record.
Each is addressed under its own standard.

B. The objections are timely.

Rule 72(a) requires objections within 14 days after service. ECF No. 84 was entered
October 7, 2026. The Court serves orders on Plaintiff by mail. ECF No. 68-1 4 3. Plaintiff
submitted these objections on October 13, 2026. That submission is within fourteen days of the
entry date itself, without the additional time Rule 6(d) provides for mail service. Plaintiff does not
rely on the later date.

C. Alternative classification.

Amendment and preconference discovery are pretrial matters within § 636(b)(1)(A).
Plaintiff presents these objections under Rule 72(a). To the extent the Court treats any portion of
ECF No. 84 as dispositive of a claim or defense, Plaintiff alternatively requests treatment of that
portion under 28 U.S.C. § 636(b)(1)(B){C) and de novo determination under Rule 72(b)(3).
Plaintiff does not contend that ECF No. 84 terminated any claim. The proposed pleading adds no
defendant, no cause of action, and no category of relief; it retains the six-count structure of the First
Amended Complaint. ECF No. 59 {{ 3-6.

D. The concurrent applications do not replace these objections.

Plaintiff concurrently presents a motion under 28 U.S.C. § 455 concerning the Magistrate
Judge’s disqualification and a motion to the District Judge for targeted vacatur and withdrawal or

modification of the referral. Those applications neither replace these objections nor extend their

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document91 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 4 of 29 PagelD# 908

filing period. The grounds and affirmative relief presented in these objections remain
independently maintained. Rule 72(a) provides that a party “may not assign as error a defect in the
order not timely objected to.” These objections are filed within the Rule 72(a) period and preserve
every defect identified here.

Il. THE DISCOVERY MOTIONS INVOKED AUTHORITY THAT ECF NO. 84
TREATED AS UNAVAILABLE
A. The Order’s stated reason is categorical, and the rule contains the exception
the motions invoked.

“A party may not seek discovery from any source before the parties have conferred as
required by Rule 26(f), except in a proceeding exempted from initial disclosure under Rule 26(a)(1)
(B), or when authorized by these rules, by stipulation, or by court order.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d)(1).
The first clause states the restriction. The last clause states the exception. Both Defendants quoted
that exception in their oppositions. ECF No. 33 at 3; ECF No. 73 at 2. Their dispute concerned
entitlement, not the existence of authority.

ECF No. 84 did not decide entitlement. It stated: “At this time, the Court cannot issue an
order concerning Plaintiff’s Motions because discovery has not officially begun in this case.
Pursuant to the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, discovery officially begins when the District
Judge issues a Scheduling Order and currently there is no Scheduling Order in this case.” ECF No.
84 at 1-2. The rule keys its restriction to the Rule 26(f) conference, not to a Scheduling Order, and
excepts a court order from the restriction. A court may evaluate a request for that order and decline
it. A court may not treat the restriction as the answer to a request for the exception. A ruling that
“relies on erroneous factual or legal premises” is contrary to law. Wall, 42 F.4th at 220. Plaintiff
contends only that the Order’s expressed reason is categorical.

B. The requests are closed, limited, and directed to records only Defendants hold.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document91 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 5 of 29 PagelD# 909

ECF Nos. 15 and 15-1 propose three interrogatories to NCMEC. Each asks whether one of
the two CyberTipline reports referenced in NCMEC’s April 22, 2026 letters, “as originally
received by NCMEC,” contained or otherwise identified “Marvelle J. Ballentine,” “Jay
Ballentine,” or jaychizza@icloud.com. Each excludes information supplied by Plaintiff in the
April 9, 2026 materials, court filings, public sources, and information obtained or added after
original receipt.

ECF Nos. 54 and 54-1 propose four interrogatories to Meta. They ask whether, between
July 1, 2022 and April 22, 2026, Meta submitted to NCMEC a CyberTipline report in connection
with the Facebook account associated with Plaintiff and terminated on or about July 4, 2022, and
whether any such report contained or otherwise identified each of the three identifiers. A Meta
submission is not assumed to be either report referenced in NCMEC’s letters.

The same limitations govern both sets. Answers are limited to “Yes,” “No,” or “Unable to
determine after reasonable inquiry.” No explanation, report content, report-by-report mapping, or
determination of personal identity from a name alone is requested. Each motion asks that answers
be served within seven calendar days after service. ECF No. 15 at 2-3; ECF No. 54 at 3. Neither
motion seeks the reports, depositions, documents, metadata, or any follow-up discovery. An
answer of “Unable to determine” fixes one fact about the state of the responding party’s records
and establishes nothing about liability.

C. The existing showing supports authorization.

The April 22, 2026 letters associated two CyberTipline reports with the three identifiers
Plaintiff had supplied in his April 9, 2026 materials, joined by “and/or.” ECF No. 60 at 8; ECF No.
59-1 § J. NCMEC’s dismissal memorandum asserts that the statements in the letters are true, states
that Plaintiff “does not have access to those reports,” and describes the asserted linkage as

involving Plaintiff, “a person with the same name,” or an e-mail address. ECF No. 74 at 5

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document91_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 6 of 29 PagelD# 910

(describing ECF No. 11); ECF No. 59-1 4 160; ECF No. 60 at 8. NCMEC seeks dismissal with
prejudice, and its opposition to amendment states that “[n]Jo allegations Plaintiff can make can
change that fact.” ECF No. 11 at 17; ECF No. 74 at 5. One informational gap does two jobs.
NCMEC invokes the reports’ contents to defeat the claims and invokes Plaintiff’s inability to
inspect the reports to defeat any challenge. ECF No. 78-1 at 1-2. The three answers test the first use
without requiring production of anything.

Meta’s position is parallel. Meta’s dismissal briefing characterizes the conspiracy
allegations as implausible. ECF No. 73 at 3-4 (describing ECF Nos. 21, 22, 39). Whether Meta
submitted a CyberTipline report concerning the account terminated July 4, 2022, and what
identifiers any such report carried, are facts in Meta’s records, and Meta seeks dismissal with
prejudice while those facts remain there. ECF No. 59-1 4215; ECF No. 81 at 2-6; ECF No. 55 at 4—
7.

Plaintiff’s own knowledge is on the record. Before April 22, 2026, he never used the name
“Marvelle J. Ballentine” on any Meta account; the Facebook account associated with the July 4,
2022 enforcement event was maintained under the name “Jay Ballentine”; and he supplied his legal
name in the April 9, 2026 materials because it is the name under which the two federal actions were
pending. ECF No. 31; ECF No. 59-2 ¢§ 2-10; ECF No. 60 at 7-8. That declaration supplies the
factual basis for each interrogatory.

Timing is the reason for the request now. If dismissal with prejudice is entered on the
premise of what the reports establish and Plaintiff’s inability to inspect them, no later discovery
occurs. ECF No. 16 at 4-7; ECF No. 55 at 4-7; ECF No. 78-1 at 4-6; ECF No. 81 at 2-6. No
Defendant identified a specific burden or asserted a privilege against answering. ECF No. 81 at 6.

D. The actual oppositions do not supply the reason ECF No. 84 stated.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document91_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 7 of 29 PagelD# 911

NCMEC argued that Plaintiff’s “request for discovery is to ascertain whether he has a
viable claim.” ECF No. 33 at 3. The First Amended Complaint states its claims without the
answers. The requests test an affirmative factual representation on which NCMEC seeks dismissal
with prejudice.

Meta argued that a Rule 12(b)(6) motion tests only the sufficiency of the allegations, so
discovery “would have no bearing” on its motion. ECF No. 73 at 4-5. Defendants’ motions do not
confine themselves to sufficiency. They assert the truth of the letters and Plaintiff’s lack of access
as grounds. The answers bear on whether those assertions may be accepted at this stage.
Authorization of early discovery and use of any resulting answer in deciding a pleading motion are
separate questions.

Meta urged a modified preliminary-injunction test. ECF No. 73 at 3. Plaintiff has argued
that a reasonableness or good-cause inquiry governs. ECF No. 16 at 4-7; ECF No. 55 at 4-7; ECF
No. 81 at 2-6. Under either formulation the court evaluates the request. ECF No. 84 evaluated
nothing. Plaintiff preserves his alternative showing under the stricter approach: the First Amended
Complaint pleads each claim in detail, and the harm from denial is a dismissal with prejudice
entered on an untested factual premise.

Meta noted that discovery was stayed in the earlier action, No. 1:26-cv-01341, pending
NCMEC’s motion to dismiss there, and argued that Plaintiff may seek discovery later if his claims
survive. ECF No. 73 at 5. The earlier action was voluntarily dismissed, and a stay of general
discovery entered on that record does not decide a request for seven closed answers in this one.
ECF No. 84 did not rely on it. The requests are directed to the premise on which dismissal with
prejudice is sought. A ruling on that premise before the answers exist is the harm the timing

argument identifies.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document91_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 8 of 29 PagelD# 912

E. Relief and independence.

Plaintiff requests that the Court authorize the interrogatories on the existing showing.
Alternatively, Plaintiff requests that the Court set aside the denials and direct determination of ECF
Nos. 15 and 54 under Rule 26(d)(1), preserving their briefing. Both motions rest on the First
Amended Complaint and the existing record, and the requested answers remain supported whether
or not leave to amend is granted. ECF Nos. 16, 55.

IV. THE RECORD BEFORE ECF NO. 84 CONTAINED A COMPLETED
SUBMISSION AND UNRESOLVED REQUESTS CONCERNING THE
CONDITION

September 7-8. Plaintiff submitted the motion for leave to amend and supplement through
the Electronic Document Submission System on September 7, 2026. ECF No. 68-1 4] 5. The Clerk
docketed it September 8 as ECF No. 59, with the complete proposed Second Amended and
Supplemental Complaint (ECF No. 59-1), a supporting declaration (ECF No. 59-2), a
memorandum identifying the material amendments by category and section (ECF No. 60), anda
notice waiving oral argument and requesting determination on the papers (ECF No. 61).

September 9. ECF No. 64 found that the Court “does not possess sufficient information to
issue an Order on this matter.” It directed Plaintiff to provide “a redlined version of the Amended
Complaint [Dkt. Nos. 59-1, 60-1], no later than September 11, 2026,” that “must clearly indicate
the changes, deletions, and additions that were made to Plaintiff’s Complaint [Dkt. No. 1].” ECF
No. 64. It stated no consequence for nonproduction.

September 11. Plaintiff first learned of ECF No. 64 at about 9:09 p.m. Eastern Time,
through a CourtListener docket alert. ECF No. 68-1 4 8-9. Plaintiff is not a registered CM/ECF

user and receives court orders by mail; no mailed copy had arrived as of September 13. Id. 1] 3, 10.

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document91 _ Filed 10/13/26 Page 9 of 29 PagelD# 913

September 13-14. Plaintiff submitted his objections to ECF Nos. 63-65 and his motion to
set aside ECF No. 64 on September 13. ECF No. 67 4 5. The Clerk docketed them September 14.
ECF Nos. 66, 67, 68, 68-1. They objected to the information-sufficiency finding, the comparison
against ECF No. 1, and the September 11 deadline. ECF No. 67 4 1. They requested suspension of
enforcement during review, relief from the expired deadline under Rule 6(b)(1)(B), and, if a
comparison requirement were sustained, an order identifying the baseline with seven calendar days
after actual notice to comply. ECF No. 67 {§ 6(b), 7; ECF No. 68 at 3-12.

September 18. NCMEC and Hall opposed amendment. ECF No. 74. The opposition stated
that “Plaintiff’s failure to timely file the ordered document is understandable based on his
representations as to not receiving notifications,” reported that counsel “has been unable to
‘reverse-engineer’ a redline comparison of the two documents via either Adobe or Word,” and
requested “the opportunity to supplement or amend this Opposition, if and when Plaintiff submits
the redline version.” ECF No. 74 at 4. Plaintiff sought leave to present the comparison-difficulty
statement in connection with the pending objections. ECF No. 76 (submitted September 18,
docketed September 22).

September 22. ECF No. 82 accepted ECF Nos. 78 and 78-1 as a reply to both NCMEC’s
discovery opposition (ECF No. 33) and NCMEC and Hall’s amendment opposition (ECF No. 74).
Meta opposed amendment the same day. ECF No. 83.

October 7. ECF No. 84 denied ECF No. 59 for nonproduction “as of the date of this Order”
and denied ECF Nos. 15 and 54 as premature. The docket reflects no determination of ECF Nos.
66, 67, or 76, of the suspension request, or of the Rule 6(b)(1)(B) request before that date. On

October 12, 2026, Plaintiff submitted a Notice of Waiver of Oral Argument as to ECF Nos. 66, 67,

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document91_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 10 of 29 PagelD#
914

and 76, requesting determination of those motions on the papers under Local Civil Rule 7(J). That
submission postdates ECF No. 84.

ECF No. 82 has one significance here. Plaintiff does not contend that it extended the
deadline, suspended ECF No. 64, or authorized withholding the comparison. He contends that the
amendment motion was treated as live and briefed on its merits through September 22, and was
then denied without reaching them.

Vv. THE COMPARISON CONDITION MUST BE EVALUATED AGAINST THE
SUBMITTED INFORMATION AND THE SELECTED BASELINE
A. The stated premise was insufficient information, and the record supplied
substantial information.

ECF No. 64 rests on one finding: the Court “does not possess sufficient information to issue
an Order on this matter.” Four documents were before the Court when that finding was made. The
proposed pleading was filed in full; it rans 297 paragraphs. ECF No. 59-1; ECF No. 74 at 2. A
declaration supporting the new account-name allegations was filed. ECF No. 59-2. A twenty-page
memorandum stated that the proposed pleading “does five principal things” and located each by
section. ECF No. 60 at 2-3, 7-14. The pleading to be replaced was on the docket. ECF No. 5. ECF
No. 60 does not display every wording change. It identifies the material amendments by category
and section. The additional requirement should be assessed against that information.

B. The selected baseline combines two sets of changes.

ECF No. 59 seeks to replace the First Amended Complaint. ECF No. 5; ECF No. 59 3.
ECF No. 64 required comparison against the original Complaint. ECF No. 1. A comparison against
ECF No. 1 displays the amendments made when the First Amended Complaint was filed and the
amendments now proposed, merged. It does not isolate the changes the motion asks the Court to
evaluate. The required document would not supply the information a comparison exists to supply.

ECF No. 68 at 8-12. Plaintiff does not contend that a historical comparison can never serve a case-

10

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document91_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 11 of 29 PagelD#
915

management purpose. He contends that this cumulative comparison was not the appropriate
prerequisite to considering this motion on this record.

C. The governing limits on case-specific procedural directions.

A judge “may regulate practice in any manner consistent with federal law, rules adopted
under 28 U.S.C. §§ 2072 and 2075, and the district’s local rules.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 83(b). The same
rule provides that “[nJo sanction or other disadvantage may be imposed for noncompliance with
any requirement not in federal law, federal rules, or the local rules unless the alleged violator has
been furnished in the particular case with actual notice of the requirement.” Id. The Supreme Court
has identified two limits on a court’s case-management power: the exercise must be a “reasonable
response to the problems and needs” confronting the court’s fair administration of justice, and “the
power cannot contradict any express rule or statute.” Dietz v. Bouldin, 579 U.S. 40, 45-46 (2016).

Plaintiff does not contend that the Magistrate Judge lacked authority to request a
comparison. Plaintiff had actual notice of the direction as of 9:09 p.m. on September 11, so the
actual-notice condition in Rule 83(b) does not by itself defeat the October 7 denial. Its function is to
secure an opportunity to comply before a disadvantage attaches. The opportunity actually afforded
is the subject of Part VI.

D. The connection between the requirement and the denial.

The requirement added a cumulative document measured against a superseded pleading,
with two days to produce it, and the consequence attached was exclusion of the completed
submission from consideration. The question is whether the informational value of the additional
document, measured against what the Court already had, justified withholding consideration of
ECF No. 59 when the condition was under challenge, relief from its deadline was pending, and a

prospective procedure had been proposed. ECF No. 84 does not address that question.

11

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document91_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 12 of 29 PagelD#
916

VI. THE ORIGINAL DEADLINE AND THE LATER NONPRODUCTION REQUIRE
DIFFERENT ASSESSMENTS
ECF No. 84 found that Plaintiff “was given ample opportunity to comply.” ECF No. 84 at 2.

The finding spans September 9 through October 7. Two periods inside it present different
questions.

A. The initial opportunity ended late on the compliance date.

ECF No. 64 was entered Wednesday, September 9. It set a deadline of Friday, September
11. Plaintiff first received actual notice at about 9:09 p.m. on September 11. ECF No. 68-1 {ff 8-9.
The preparation opportunity remaining after actual notice was the remainder of that evening.
NCMEC’s own opposition states that “Plaintiff’s failure to timely file the ordered document is
understandable based on his representations as to not receiving notifications.” ECF No. 74 at 4.
Plaintiff uses that concession for the initial period only; it is not a concession of excusable neglect
or an excuse extending to October 7.

B. Relief from the expired deadline was requested within two days and was never
decided.

Rule 6(b)(1)(B) permits an extension after a deadline has expired “if the party failed to act
because of excusable neglect.” The determination “is at bottom an equitable one, taking account of
all relevant circumstances surrounding the party’s omission,” including “the danger of prejudice,”

2) 66.

“the length of the delay and its potential impact on judicial proceedings,” “the reason for the delay,
including whether it was within the reasonable control of the movant,” and “whether the movant
acted in good faith.” Pioneer Inv. Servs. Co. v. Brunswick Assocs. Ltd. P’ship, 507 U.S. 380, 395
(1993). The Fourth Circuit treats the reason for the delay as “[t]he most important of the factors.”
Thompson v. E.I. DuPont de Nemours & Co., 76 F.3d 530, 534 (4th Cir. 1996). Plaintiff requested
Rule 6(b)(1)(B) relief on September 13. ECF No. 67 7; ECF No. 68 at 7-8. Each factor is renewed

here.

12

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document91_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 13 of 29 PagelD#
917

Prejudice. No opposition to ECF No. 59 was due on September 11. No Defendant has
identified harm from the timing of a comparison. NCMEC’s opposition describes the document as
one that “would allow the litigants and the Court the opportunity to easily see what changes have
been made,” and asks to supplement its opposition “if and when” a comparison is filed. ECF No. 74
at 4. That is a request for convenience and a workable course, not a claim of prejudice.

Length and impact. The interval between actual notice and the request for relief was two
days. Less than three hours remained in the compliance date when actual notice arrived. ECF No.
68-1 §§ 8-9. The amendment motion remained the subject of authorized briefing through
September 22. ECF No. 82.

Reason and reasonable control. The reason for the initial failure is sworn. Plaintiff receives
orders by mail and supplements mail service with periodic docket review; he was unwell from
about September 7 through the afternoon of September 11 and directed that no review occur during
that period. ECF No. 68-1 §§ 3-6, 10. The method and timing of the Court’s service were outside
Plaintiff’s control. The decision not to review the docket during the sworn period of illness was his.
The combination left no meaningful opportunity to comply before the deadline expired.

Good faith. Plaintiff disclosed the chronology under oath, sought relief within two days,
and proposed a specific compliance procedure. ECF No. 67 4 7; ECF No. 68-1. The request was
never ruled on. ECF No. 84 did not deny it. ECF No. 84 proceeded as though it had been denied.

C. The continued nonproduction is acknowledged, and it did not by itself
establish that denial was the appropriate consequence.

No comparison was produced between September 11 and October 7. Plaintiff states that
without qualification. Objections to a nondispositive order do not stay it. Plant v. Merrifield Town
Ctr. Ltd. P’ship, 711 F. Supp. 2d 576, 584-85 (E.D. Va. 2010) (“[T]here is no support for the

contention that a magistrate judge’s order on a nondispositive motion . . . is automatically stayed

13

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document91_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 14 of 29 PagelD#
918

upon timely filing of an objection to that order.”). ECF No. 64 remained enforceable throughout the
period. Plaintiff does not contend otherwise.

What occurred in that period is established by the chronology in Part IV: review of the
condition was sought, relief from the deadline and a prospective procedure were requested,
counsel’s comparison-difficulty statement was presented, and further briefing was accepted. Those
requests did not excuse compliance. They bear on the appropriate response to noncompliance. A
party whose request for relief from a deadline is pending has not been told that the request is
denied, has not been told that a different deadline applies, and has not been told what consequence
will follow. ECF No. 84 supplied all three answers at once, by denying the motion.

Plant recommended sanctions against a party that had repeatedly failed to respond to
discovery after objections with no staying effect. 711 F. Supp. 2d at 584-86. It did not hold that
every period of noncompliance during pending objections requires the most consequential
available response. Plant marks the difference between enforceability, which Plaintiff concedes,
and the selection of a consequence, which is the question here. Elapsed time neither resolved the
pending requests nor established that exclusion of the completed submission was the appropriate
consequence. ECF No. 84 treated it as doing both.

D. ECF No. 59 should be determined on the existing submission.

Plaintiff requests that ECF No. 59 be determined on the existing complete submission
without an additional comparison. The proposed pleading, the supporting declaration, and the
memorandum locating the material amendments by category and section are on the docket. ECF
Nos. 59-1, 59-2, 60. Any order setting aside the denial should expressly vacate the comparison
requirement and the September 11 deadline, so that the restored motion is not subject to the same

condition.

14

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document91_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 15 of 29 PagelD#
919

Vil. THE STATED PROCEDURAL REASON SHOULD NOT EXCLUDE THIS
AMENDMENT-AND-SUPPLEMENTATION SUBMISSION
A. Both forms of leave were requested, and each requires a reason bearing on the
request.

“The court should freely give leave when justice so requires.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a)(2). Rule
15(d) permits a supplemental pleading for events “that happened after the date of the pleading to be
supplemented,” and the standards for the two motions “are nearly identical.” Franks v. Ross, 313
F.3d 184, 198 n.15 (4th Cir. 2002). Leave “should be denied only when the amendment would be
prejudicial to the opposing party, there has been bad faith on the part of the moving party, or the
amendment would have been futile.” Laber v. Harvey, 438 F.3d 404, 426 (4th Cir. 2006) (en banc).
“[OJutright refusal to grant the leave without any justifying reason appearing for the denial is not an
exercise of discretion; it is merely abuse of that discretion and inconsistent with the spirit of the
Federal Rules.” Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178, 182 (1962).

Foman does not exempt a movant from valid procedural orders. It requires that a denial rest
on an apparent or declared reason that justifies it. Plaintiff does not contend that noncompliance
with a procedural direction can never justify denying leave. He contends that nonproduction of this
cumulative comparison, on the record stated in Parts IV through VI, did not justify excluding this
completed submission.

The nature and timing of the proposed changes bear on every Rule 15 factor. The proposed
pleading adds no defendant, no cause of action, and no category of relief; it retains the six counts of
the First Amended Complaint. ECF No. 59 {ff 3—6. It strengthens the falsity allegations,
incorporates post-filing events, and adds factual support to existing counts. ECF No. 60 at 2—3. It

was submitted on September 7, twenty-six days after the first dismissal motion, before any answer,

15

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD Document91_ Filed 10/13/26 Page 16 of 29 PagelD#
920

Rule 26(f) conference, discovery, or Scheduling Order. ECF No. 84 at 1-2. The supplemental
matter concerns events after August 6, 2026. ECF No. 59 45.

B. No warning preceded the consequence, and a less severe course was already on
the docket.
ECF No. 64 did not state that nonproduction would result in denial of ECF No. 59. The

Section 455(b)(4) requires disqualification where a magistrate judge knows that he has a
financial interest in a party, “however small.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(4), (d)(4). Section 455(a)
requires disqualification where impartiality might reasonably be questioned, an objective inquiry
that does not depend on the judge’s knowledge. Liljeberg v. Health Servs. Acquisition Corp., 486
U.S. 847, 859-60 (1988). The manner in which the interest is held, the dates of ownership, and any
exception under § 455(d)(4)(i) or § 455(f) are matters requiring determination.

Plaintiff was unaware of the reported interest when ECF No. 84 was entered and presents
this ground promptly after learning of it. Declaration of Marvelle J. Ballentine in Support of
Plaintiff’s Motion to Disqualify {§ 2-4. Plaintiff requests express consideration of Exhibits A and
B and the Declaration on this limited issue, or alternatively adjudication of this ground through the
concurrent Motion for Targeted Vacatur of ECF Nos. 64 and 84, so that its determination does not
depend exclusively on the scope of ordinary Rule 72(a) record review.

Section 455 “neither prescribes nor prohibits any particular remedy.” Liljeberg, 486 U.S. at
862. Vacatur turns on “the risk of injustice to the parties in the particular case, the risk that the
denial of relief will produce injustice in other cases, and the risk of undermining the public’s
confidence in the judicial process.” Id. at 864. Plaintiff requests vacatur of ECF No. 84 upon the
necessary statutory and remedial findings. Plaintiff does not contend that ECF No. 84 is void. This
objection supplements the four preceding objections, which remain independently presented with
their affirmative relief, and its pendency does not prevent the District Judge from granting relief
independently warranted on them.

B. The balance of interests.

A pause in proceedings “calls for the exercise of judgment, which must weigh competing
interests and maintain an even balance,” and “the suppliant for a stay must make out a clear case of
hardship or inequity in being required to go forward, if there is even a fair possibility that the stay

55 (1936). The Fourth Circuit places the burden on the party seeking the pause. Williford v.
Armstrong World Indus., Inc., 715 F.2d 124, 127 (4th Cir. 1983).

Deferring claim-terminating adjudication of ECF Nos. 10, 21, and 45 postpones decision
on motions that are fully briefed, and Defendants’ interest in prompt resolution is affected. The
sequence is nevertheless justified. The hardship is specific: claim-terminating adjudication on a
pleading Plaintiff has moved to replace, while the condition that excluded the replacement is before
this Court on timely objections. A ruling entered in that posture must be revisited if the objections
are sustained. The matters may be determined together in one order; the request is for order of
decision, not for a separate waiting period. The comparison-condition protection affects no interest
of Defendants beyond timing. ECF No. 74 at 4. The existing briefing on every affected motion is
preserved, and the period is defined by identified decisions.
